questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'Have you ever seen ___ volcano?'
questions.context: You mention one thing that you have never seen before.

options.text: a
options.feedback: Correct. 'A volcano' introduces a single thing for the first time, which is exactly what the indefinite article does.

options.text: some
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Some' would not normally be used with a singular countable noun in this question.

options.text: an
options.feedback: Wrong. 'An' is required before a vowel sound and volcano begins with a consonant sound.

options.text: the
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The volcano' assumes the listener already knows which volcano is meant.

questions.explanation:
The indefinite article a or an introduces something new, while the definite article the points to something already identified.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct article before the word 'orange'.
questions.context: You mention one thing for the first time, and its name starts with a vowel sound.

options.text: a orange
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A orange' would be correct before a consonant sound but not before this vowel sound.

options.text: an orange
options.feedback: Correct. The choice between a and an depends on the sound, and orange begins with a vowel sound.

options.text: some orange
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Some' is normally used with plural or uncountable nouns and not with a single countable item.

options.text: the orange
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The orange' presupposes a specific orange already known to the listener.

questions.explanation:
The article is decided by the initial sound of the following word, not by the letter, which is why an hour and a university both take a.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: '___ water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius.'
questions.context: You introduce a general concept.

options.text: A water
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A water' would treat the noun as countable, which it is not.

options.text: The water
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The water' refers to a specific body of water already identified in the context.

options.text: Water
options.feedback: Correct. When a statement is true of all instances of a noun, English normally omits the article altogether.

options.text: Some waters
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Some waters' pluralises an uncountable noun, which is not permitted here.

questions.explanation:
General statements about uncountable nouns such as water take no article at all, which is one of the commonest examination traps.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the question with the correct article.
questions.context: A classmate asks about something you do not know.

options.text: What time does film start?
options.feedback: Wrong. Leaving the article out makes the sentence ungrammatical for a countable noun.

options.text: What time does the a film start?
options.feedback: Wrong. The two articles together contradict each other and cannot modify the same noun.

options.text: What time does a film start?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A film' would introduce a different film each time, which is not the meaning of the question.

options.text: What time does the film start?
options.feedback: Correct. 'The film' refers to a specific film that both speakers are discussing, so the definite article is required.

questions.explanation:
A question about a mutually identified item takes the definite article, whereas asking about any instance of a class would take an indefinite one.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'The sun rises in the ___.'
questions.context: A description refers to something unique in the world.

options.text: east
options.feedback: Correct. In geographical expressions such as 'in the east', the definite article precedes the direction word.

options.text: east's
options.feedback: Wrong. A possessive ending cannot be attached to a direction word in this phrase.

options.text: an east
options.feedback: Wrong. 'An east' is not a standard expression for a direction.

options.text: the east
options.feedback: Wrong. Omitting the article is unusual in this fixed geographical construction.

questions.explanation:
Directions are unusual because they take the definite article when used as noun phrases, unlike most uncountable general references.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly refers to meals as a class.
questions.context: A speaker mentions meals in general.

options.text: The breakfast is usually served at seven.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The breakfast' refers to a particular meal already mentioned.

options.text: Breakfast is usually served at seven.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Breakfast' used in this general sense takes no article, which is the standard pattern for meal names.

options.text: Breakfasts are usually served at seven in Peru.
options.feedback: Wrong. Pluralising meal names in this sense is not standard English and would refer to individual portions.

options.text: A breakfast is usually served at seven.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A breakfast' counts a single instance rather than referring to the meal as a general category.

questions.explanation:
Meal names such as breakfast, lunch and dinner take the definite article only when referring to a specific meal, not when used generally.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses the correct article for a general statement about hospitals.
questions.context: A sentence mentions a hospital, and the speaker wants to generalise.

options.text: A hospitals usually have a qualified staff.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A hospitals' is impossible because the indefinite article cannot modify a plural noun.

options.text: The hospitals usually have a qualified staff.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The hospitals' points to particular hospitals already identified.

options.text: Hospitals usually have a qualified staff.
options.feedback: Correct. A general statement about all hospitals takes the plural noun without an article.

options.text: Hospital usually have a qualified staff.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Hospital' without a determiner and with a plural verb is ungrammatical here.

questions.explanation:
General plural references to institutions take no article, whereas specific institutions referred to individually take the definite article.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the statement that best describes the zero article.
questions.context: A grammar handbook explains when the zero article is used.

options.text: It is used only with plural nouns and never with singular ones.
options.feedback: Wrong. The zero article is also used with singular uncountable nouns and with some singular proper names.

options.text: It is never used with proper names in English.
options.feedback: Wrong. Many proper names, such as city names and the names of rivers, normally take no article at all.

options.text: It is used with any singular countable noun that has not been mentioned before.
options.feedback: Wrong. A singular countable noun requires an article; the indefinite article is exactly what this rule rules out.

options.text: It is used with uncountable nouns in general statements and with many fixed expressions and proper names.
options.feedback: Correct. This accurately lists the main contexts, since the zero article covers general uncountables, fixed phrases and many proper names.

questions.explanation:
The zero article is defined by what it excludes, so describing it accurately requires covering both its genuine uses and the cases it cannot cover.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the version with the correct article before the country name.
questions.context: An editor checks a sentence about a country.

options.text: Peru is in the west of South America.
options.feedback: Correct. Most country names take the zero article, so no article is needed before Peru.

options.text: Peru are in the west of South America.
options.feedback: Wrong. The subject is singular, so the verb must be 'is' rather than 'are'.

options.text: A Peru is in the west of South America.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A Peru' would imply that Peru were one country among several unnamed ones.

options.text: The Peru is in the west of South America.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The Peru' is not used; the article does not appear with the name of this country.

questions.explanation:
Country names usually take no article, though a few such as the Netherlands and the Philippines are well-known exceptions.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that uses the correct article in a fixed expression.
questions.context: A grammar task tests a fixed expression that includes an article.

options.text: I go to the school by bus every day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The school' would refer to a specific building and would change the meaning entirely.

options.text: I go to school by bus every day.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Go to school' is a fixed expression meaning to attend school as a pupil, and it takes no article.

options.text: I go to school on bus every day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'On bus' is not a valid prepositional phrase; transport by bus uses 'by'.

options.text: I go to a school by bus every day.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A school' would introduce one unspecified school, which is not what the expression means.

questions.explanation:
Fixed expressions such as go to school, go to bed and go to church describe activities rather than places and never take an article.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'I have ___ brother and ___ sister.'
questions.context: A classmate asks about your family.

options.text: an; a
options.feedback: Wrong. 'An brother' is incorrect because brother begins with a consonant sound.

options.text: a; an
options.feedback: Wrong. 'An sister' is incorrect because sister begins with a consonant sound.

options.text: a; a
options.feedback: Correct. The indefinite article is used before both nouns because brother and the first mention of sister are both new information beginning with consonants.

options.text: the; a
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The brother' would imply a brother already identified, which the sentence does not establish.

questions.explanation:
Each singular countable noun needs its own determiner, so a repeated noun in the same sentence takes the article again.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses each and every with singular nouns.
questions.context: A sentence refers to a sequence of institutions.

options.text: Each of the candidates and every of the panel were interviewed.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Every of the panel' is not a valid construction, because every cannot be followed by of.

options.text: Each of the candidate and every members of the panel were interviewed.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Each of the candidate' needs the plural noun, and 'every members' wrongly pluralises after every.

options.text: Each of the candidates and every member of the panel was interviewed.
options.feedback: Wrong. A plural verb is used where both subjects are grammatically singular, so the agreement is wrong.

options.text: Each of the candidates and every member of the panel were interviewed.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Each of' and 'every' are both singular determiners, so the singular verb 'was' is the correct agreement.

questions.explanation:
Each and every behave like singular determiners for the purposes of subject-verb agreement, which is a standard examination point.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the zero article with a mode of transport.
questions.context: A speaker compares two ways of travelling to school.

options.text: I go to work by bicycle on Tuesdays.
options.feedback: Correct. Modes of transport such as bicycle, bus and train take the zero article in the phrase 'by bicycle'.

options.text: I go to work by a bicycle on Tuesdays.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'By a bicycle' also refers to a specific or unspecified bicycle, not to the general activity.

options.text: I go to work by the bicycle on Tuesdays.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'By the bicycle' would refer to a particular bicycle rather than the mode of transport.

options.text: I go to work on bicycle on Tuesdays.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'On bicycle' is not a valid combination of preposition and noun in this meaning.

questions.explanation:
By plus a mode of transport refers to the activity rather than to a vehicle, so it follows the same pattern as go by train.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the definite article with an abstract noun.
questions.context: An exercise tests articles before abstract nouns.

options.text: The music is important in Peruvian culture.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The music' would refer to a particular piece or body of music already under discussion.

options.text: Music is important in Peruvian culture.
options.feedback: Correct. When music refers to the whole field or activity in general, English takes the zero article.

options.text: Musics are important in Peruvian culture.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Musics' pluralises an uncountable noun, which English does not allow here.

options.text: A music is important in Peruvian culture.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A music' is ungrammatical because music is uncountable and has no plural form.

questions.explanation:
Abstract and mass nouns take the zero article in general statements but the definite article when a specific instance is intended.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a possessive determiner.
questions.context: A grammar task tests possessive determiners.

options.text: This is a notebook of mine here.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A' cannot be inserted between a possessive determiner and the noun it accompanies.

options.text: This is the notebook of me.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Of me' reverses the correct order, which requires a noun before of and a pronoun after it.

options.text: This is my notebook.
options.feedback: Correct. 'My' is a possessive determiner that goes directly before the noun without an article.

options.text: This is my a notebook.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'My a notebook' stacks two determiners before one noun, which is not permitted in English.

questions.explanation:
English allows only one determiner before a noun, and possessive determiners occupy that single slot on their own.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the revision with the correct article usage.
questions.context: An editor corrects an article error in a paragraph about schools.

options.text: The school we attend is the nearest to the city centre's.
options.feedback: Wrong. A possessive ending cannot replace the preposition in a superlative comparison.

options.text: The school we attend is the nearest to a city centre.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A city centre' would refer to some unspecified centre rather than the one being compared.

options.text: The school we attend is nearest to the city centre.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is nearest' omits the article that the superlative requires.

options.text: The school we attend is the nearest to the city centre.
options.feedback: Correct. The superlative takes the definite article, and the comparison is completed with the preposition to plus a definite noun phrase.

questions.explanation:
A superlative needs the definite article, and the phrase after the comparative preposition must also be definite for the comparison to make sense.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a determiner of quantity.
questions.context: An exam tests a determiner that indicates a limited quantity.

options.text: I have a lot of work to do this week.
options.feedback: Correct. 'A lot of' is a quantity determiner that takes an uncountable noun such as work.

options.text: I have the lot of work to do this week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The lot of' would refer to a specific known quantity and does not function as a general quantity phrase.

options.text: I have a lot of many work to do this week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A lot of many' stacks two quantifiers before a single noun, which is ungrammatical.

options.text: I have lot of work to do this week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Lot of' requires the article, since a lot of is a determiner and not a bare noun phrase.

questions.explanation:
Quantity determiners such as a lot of, a few of and plenty of each occupy the single determiner slot before their noun.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement best describes the article in the sentence 'She has been studying at the university since 2019'?
questions.context: A semantics exercise examines article use with institution names.

options.text: The article should be zero because no institution is named in the sentence.
options.feedback: Wrong. The zero article is used with general plurals such as universities, not with a single institution the speaker has in mind.

options.text: The university is specific, because it is the one where she is registered, which is why the definite article is used.
options.feedback: Correct. Definite articles are used for institutions whose identity is fixed by context or general knowledge, not only when they are named.

options.text: The article is wrong because institutions are never referred to with the definite article.
options.feedback: Wrong. Institutions are routinely referred to with the definite article whenever they are identifiable.

options.text: The article should be an indefinite one because a new institution is being introduced.
options.feedback: Wrong. An indefinite article would suggest any university rather than the particular one the speaker means.

questions.explanation:
Definiteness depends on identifiability rather than on whether a name is spelled out, which is why institutions take the.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is both grammatical and free of an unnecessary article?
questions.context: A style task asks for the most economical accurate version.

options.text: A life of nurse involves night shifts.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A life of nurse' lacks the article that the singular countable noun nurse requires.

options.text: The life of a nurse involves the night shifts.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The night shifts' restricts the reference to particular shifts, adding an article the sentence does not need.

options.text: The life of a nurse involves night shifts.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Night shifts' in the general sense takes no article, and 'a nurse' correctly introduces one unspecified member of the profession.

options.text: The life of the a nurse involves night shifts.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The a nurse' contains two articles before one noun, which is never possible.

questions.explanation:
Economy in article use means removing the article that general and plural references do not require, without removing those they do.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which both articles are correct.
questions.context: An exam tests articles in a sentence with two nouns.

options.text: The head of the department the resigned yesterday.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The department the resigned' inserts an extra article and leaves the structure with two determiners.

options.text: Head of the department resigned yesterday.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Head of the department' lacks the article before the singular noun head, which is required.

options.text: The head of department resigned yesterday.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Of department' lacks the article before a singular countable noun used as a role or institution.

options.text: The head of the department resigned yesterday.
options.feedback: Correct. 'The head' takes the definite article because the role is unique, and 'the department' is also identifiable in the context.

questions.explanation: Roles and institutions are singular countable nouns, so each one needs its own determiner and cannot share a single one.
